## Part 1: Fundamentals

## What Are Multi-Agent Systems?

Multi-agent systems consist of multiple independent AI actors powered by language models, connected through coordination mechanisms. The key distinction from single-agent systems is dividing cognitive labor among specialized agents rather than having one generalist handle everything.

## Anatomy of a Multi-Agent System

Every multi-agent system has four core components:

| Component              | Description                                                                 |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Agents                 | Independent units, each with their own LLM, prompt, tools, and state access |
| Coordination Mechanism | How agents communicate and route work to each other                         |
| State Management       | Persistent information shared across agent interactions                     |
| Entry/Exit Points      | Interface with users - where requests come in and responses go out          |

## Single Agent vs Multi-Agent

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Comparing Single Agent vs Multi-Agent architecture

## When Does Multi-Agent Make Sense?

## The Five Triggers

Consider multi-agent architecture when you encounter any of these situations:

| Trigger               | Symptom                                      | Why Multi-Agent Helps                               |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Tool Overload         | Agent with 30+ tools makes poor tool choices | Specialists have focused toolsets, better selection |
| Context Window Limits | Quality degrades as conversation grows       | Context isolation prevents bloat                    |

| Sequential Constraints    | Must enforce "do X before Y" architecturally     | Handoffs or workflows enforce order    |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Parallelization Needs     | Independent subtasks need simultaneous execution | Parallel dispatch reduces latency      |
| Organizational Boundaries | Different teams own different capabilities       | Separate agents for separate ownership |

## When to Stay Single-Agent

Don't over-engineer. Stay with a single agent when:

- Simple, focused tasks with fewer than 15 tools
- Tight latency requirements (multi-agent adds overhead)
- Limited budget (more agents = more LLM calls)
- Early development stage (start simple, add complexity when needed)

## Benefits vs Tradeoffs

## Benefits

| Benefit                 | Description                                       |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Better Accuracy         | Specialized prompts improve domain performance    |
| Improved Tool Selection | Fewer tools per agent = better choices            |
| Maintainability         | Modular agents are easier to update independently |
| Parallel Execution      | Some patterns enable simultaneous processing      |
| Graceful Expansion      | Add new specialists without rewriting everything  |
| Enforced Compliance     | Architectural constraints enforce business rules  |

## Tradeoffs

| Tradeoff             | Impact                                            |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Increased Latency    | Coordination overhead adds 2-4x typical slowdown  |
| Higher Costs         | More LLM calls, potentially 2-5x cost increase    |
| More Complexity      | Harder to debug, more moving parts                |
| Context Engineering  | Must carefully design what each agent sees        |
| Coherence Challenges | Maintaining consistent conversation across agents |

## Cost Comparison (Simple Task)

| Pattern      | LLM Calls   | Relative Cost   |
|--------------|-------------|-----------------|
| Single Agent | 1-2         | Baseline        |
| SubAgents    | 3-4         | 2-3x            |
| Handoffs     | 2-3         | 1.5-2x          |
| Router       | 3-4         | 2-3x            |
| Skills       | 2-3         | 1.5-2x          |

## The Four Multi-Agent Patterns

| Pattern                                               | Core Idea                                  | Best For   |
|-------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|------------|
| Main agent calls specialists as tools                 | Complex orchestration, centralized control | SubAgents  |
| Agents transfer control via state-updating tool calls | Customer support, sequential workflows     | Handoffs   |
| Single agent loads specialized context on-demand      | Large knowledge bases, coding assistants   | Skills     |
| Classify →dispatch (parallel)→ synthesize             | Multi-domain queries, parallel research    | Router     |

## Part 2: The SubAgents Pattern

## What Is the SubAgents Pattern?

The SubAgents pattern (also called Supervisor Architecture) features a central Supervisor Agent that coordinates specialized Subagents by invoking them as tools. All routing decisions flow through the supervisor - subagents never talk to users or each other directly.

## Real-World Analogy

## CEO with Department Heads:

1. CEO (supervisor) receives all company requests
2. CEO decides which department handles what
3. Department heads (subagents) do specialized work
4. Department heads report back to CEO
5. CEO synthesizes information and responds

## Architecture Diagram

Architecture Diagram for Supervisor/SubAgents

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## Key Characteristics

| Characteristic              | Description                                 |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Centralized Control         | All routing passes through the supervisor   |
| Subagents as Tools          | Subagents invoked via tool calls            |
| No Direct User Interaction  | Subagents return results to supervisor only |
| Context Isolation           | Each subagent starts with fresh context     |
| Stateless Subagents         | Subagents don't remember previous calls     |
| Parallel Execution Possible | Supervisor can call multiple tools at once  |
| Result Synthesis            | Supervisor combines all results for user    |

## Process Flow

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Diagram for Process Flow steps

## Communication Model

| What Supervisor Sees         | What Subagent Sees             |
|------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Full conversation history    | Only the specific task input   |
| All previous tool results    | No access to main conversation |
| User preferences and context | Fresh context each invocation  |

This isolation prevents context bloat and keeps subagents focused.

## Design Decisions

## Sync vs Async Execution

| Approach     | When to Use                                        |
|--------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Synchronous  | When supervisor needs result to continue reasoning |
| Asynchronous | For long-running independent tasks                 |

## Subagent Input Options

| Option                             | Description                    | Use When                   |
|------------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Just the specific task             | Subagent needs no background   | Query only                 |
| Task plus relevant                 | Subagent benefits from context | Query + context background |
| access Access to shared state keys | Subagent needs user            | Full state                 |

## Subagent Output Options

| Option                  | Description                  | Use When             |
|-------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------|
| Just the conclusion     | Supervisor only needs result | Final answer only    |
| Result plus explanation | Debugging or transparency    | Answer + reasoning   |
| Everything subagent did | Detailed audit trail needed  | Full message history |

## Benefits

- Clear separation of concerns - each agent has focused responsibility
- Centralized orchestration - supervisor manages complexity
- Context isolation - prevents cross-domain pollution
- Parallel execution - can call multiple subagents simultaneously
- Independent development - teams can own different subagents
- Easier testing - test subagents in isolation, then integration
- Scalable - add new subagents without restructuring

## Tradeoffs

- Extra LLM call for supervisor synthesis
- No direct user interaction from subagents
- Stateless subagents can't remember previous calls
- Increased latency (sequential: supervisor → subagent → supervisor)
- Higher cost (more total tokens processed)
- Synthesis burden on supervisor
- Potential routing errors if supervisor misunderstands

## When to Use SubAgents

## ✅ Ideal Use Cases

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

| Use Case               | Why SubAgents Works                                  |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| Personal assistant     | Calendar, email, tasks are distinct domains          |
| Research workflows     | Research, analysis, writing are separate specialties |
| Customer data platform | CRM, analytics, reporting need isolation             |
| Code generation        | Planner, coder, reviewer have different focuses      |
| Multi-database queries | SQL, MongoDB, APIs need different expertise          |

## ❌ Not Suitable When

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

| Scenario                          | Better Pattern         |
|-----------------------------------|------------------------|
| Subagents need to chat with users | Handoffs               |
| Simple single-domain task         | Single agent           |
| Need persistent specialist memory | Handoffs or Skills     |
| Tight latency requirements        | Single agent or Router |

## Part 3: The Handoffs Pattern

## What Is the Handoffs Pattern?

The Handoffs pattern (also called State Machine) is where agents transfer control to each other through explicit handoff operations. Unlike SubAgents where a central supervisor coordinates, in Handoffs any agent can be the "active" agent that directly interacts with the user.

## Real-World Analogy

## Customer Support Call Center:

1. You call and reach General Support
2. They gather info, then say "Let me transfer you to Billing"
3. Billing Agent now talks to you directly
4. If needed, they connect you with Technical Support
5. Technical Agent takes over and resolves your issue

Key insight: Only one agent talks to you at a time , with explicit transfers between them.

## Architecture Diagram

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Architecture Diagram for Handoffs

## Key Characteristics

| Characteristic          | Description                                       |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Distributed Control     | No central supervisor - any agent can be active   |
| Direct User Interaction | Active agent talks directly to user               |
| Explicit Transfers      | Agents use handoff tools to transfer control      |
| Stateful Transitions    | Full state persists across agent switches         |
| Sequential Flow         | One agent active at a time (no parallelism)       |
| Conversation Continuity | Full message history available to receiving agent |

## How Handoffs Work

## The Core Mechanism

1. Agent A is active and talking to user
2. User says something requiring Agent B's expertise
3. Agent A calls a handoff tool (e.g., transfer\_to\_billing)
4. Handoff tool updates state to mark Agent B as active
5. Agent B receives full conversation and continues
6. User now talks directly with Agent B

## Process Flow Example: Customer Support

```
STEP1:WARRANTYCOLLECTOR Prompt: "Collect warranty info" Tools: [record_warranty_status] User:"My phone screen is cracked" Agent: "Is your device under warranty?" User:"Yes" Agent:*calls record_warranty_status("in_warranty")* →Updates current_step to "classification" HANDOFF STEP 2:ISSUE CLASSIFIER Prompt: "Classify the issue type" Tools: [record_issue_type] Agent:"Can you describe the issue?" User:"The screen is physically cracked" Agent:*calls record_issue_type("hardware")* →Updates current_step to "resolution" HANDOFF STEP 3:RESOLUTION SPECIALIST Prompt:"Provide resolution" Tools:[provide_solution,escalate_to_human] Agent: "Since you're in warranty with hardware damage, here's how to get a free repair..."
```

Process Flow Example (Warranty -&gt; Classifier -&gt; Resolution)

## Benefits

| Benefit                 | Description                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Direct User Interaction | Each specialist converses naturally with user |
| Sequential Enforcement  | Architecture enforces "do X before Y"         |

| Stateful Context       | Full history available to each agent             |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Natural Conversations  | Users feel like talking to different specialists |
| Flexible Navigation    | Can go back to previous steps if needed          |
| Clear Responsibilities | Each step has focused purpose                    |

## Tradeoffs

| Tradeoff             | Impact                                           |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| No Parallelism       | Only one agent active at a time                  |
| Sequential Latency   | Must complete steps in order                     |
| Context Accumulation | Message history grows (may need summarization)   |
| Handoff Overhead     | Each transfer adds a turn                        |
| User Experience      | Users notice "transfers" (can feel bureaucratic) |

## When to Use Handoffs

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## ✅ Ideal Use Cases

| Use Case           | Why Handoffs Works                        |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Customer support   | Natural transfer between departments      |
| Multi-step forms   | Collect info sequentially with validation |
| Onboarding flows   | Guide users through setup steps           |
| Approval workflows | Sequential review/approve stages          |
| Sales funnels      | Qualification →Demo→Closing               |

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

| Scenario                            | Better Pattern      |
|-------------------------------------|---------------------|
| Need parallel research              | Router or SubAgents |
| Specialists shouldn't talk to users | SubAgents           |
| Single-domain task                  | Single agent        |
| Need central synthesis              | SubAgents           |

## Handoffs vs SubAgents

| Aspect                    | Handoffs                   | SubAgents     |
|---------------------------|----------------------------|---------------|
| Distributed (any agent)   | Centralized (supervisor)   | Control       |
| Active agent directly     | Supervisor only            | User talks to |
| Stateful across transfers | Subagents stateless        | State         |
| Not supported             | Supported                  | Parallelism   |
| Shared (full history)     | Isolated (fresh each call) | Context       |
| Sequential workflows      | Parallel specialist tasks  | Best for      |

## Part 4: The Skills Pattern

## What Is the Skills Pattern?

The Skills pattern is where a single agent dynamically loads specialized instructions and tools on-demand. Instead of multiple separate agents, you have one agent that can "unlock" different capabilities when needed.

## Real-World Analogy

## A Skilled Contractor:

1. You hire a general contractor to renovate your house
2. For plumbing work, they pull out their plumbing knowledge and tools
3. For electrical work, they switch to electrical expertise
4. For carpentry, they access carpentry skills
5. It's always the same person , accessing different expertise as needed

## Architecture Diagram

Architecture Diagram for Skills Pattern

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## Key Characteristics

| Characteristic    | Description                                    |
|-------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Single Agent      | One agent instance handles everything          |
| On-Demand Loading | Skills loaded only when needed                 |
| Additive Context  | Skills add to (not replace) base instructions  |
| Tool Discovery    | Agent discovers and selects appropriate skills |
| Weak Isolation    | All skills share the same context window       |
| Low Overhead      | No inter-agent communication needed            |

## How Skills Work

## The Core Mechanism

1. Agent has base instructions and skill discovery tools
2. User makes a request
3. Agent uses get\_skills to see available skills
4. Agent uses use\_skill to load relevant skill(s)
5. Skill instructions and tools are injected into context
6. Agent completes the task with enhanced capabilities

## Process Flow Example

```
User: "what were our top 10 products by revenue last month andshow mea bar chart?" AGENT thinks:"I need SQL for data and visualization for the chart." 1.Calls get_skills() → sees available skills 2.Calls use_skill("sql_query") →loads SQL capability 3.Calls use_skill("visualization")→loads charting AGENTnowhas: ·Base tools: get_skills,use_skill SQL tools: execute_sql,list_tables,describe_table Viz tools: create_chart,export_image Agent executes query，creates chart, returns to user
```

Diagram for Skills Pattern Process Flow

## Skill Categories

| Category                  | Purpose                                     | Example          |
|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------|------------------|
| Add specialized expertise | Legal contracts, medical                    | Domain Knowledge |
| Tool Access               | Grant access to systems Database admin, API |                  |
| Add procedures            | Code review process, audit                  | Process/Workflow |

| Output Format   | Modify output style   | Technical writing, report formatting   |
|-----------------|-----------------------|----------------------------------------|

## Benefits

| Benefit              | Description                                 |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Simplicity           | Single agent, no inter-agent coordination   |
| Low Latency          | No routing overhead between agents          |
| Flexible Composition | Load multiple skills simultaneously         |
| Easy Extension       | Add new skills without restructuring        |
| Shared Context       | All skills see the full conversation        |
| Natural Flow         | No "handoffs" - feels like one conversation |
| Cost Efficient       | One agent instance, one context window      |

## Tradeoffs

| Tradeoff                | Impact                                        |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Context Window Pressure | Loaded skills consume tokens                  |
| Weak Isolation          | Skills can't have conflicting instructions    |
| No Parallelism          | Can't run skills simultaneously               |
| Tool Overload Risk      | Too many loaded skills = poor tool selection  |
| Prompt Complexity       | Base prompt + skill instructions can get long |
| No Specialization       | Same model for all domains                    |

## When to Use Skills

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## ✅ Ideal Use Cases

| Use Case            | Why Skills Works                                   |
|---------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Coding assistants   | Load language-specific skills (Python, SQL, JS)    |
| Knowledge bases     | Load domain expertise on-demand                    |
| Document processing | Load skills for different file types               |
| Data analysis       | Combine querying + visualization + interpretation  |
| Writing assistants  | Load tone/style skills (formal, casual, technical) |

## ❌ Not Suitable When

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

| Scenario                              | Better Pattern      |
|---------------------------------------|---------------------|
| Skills need parallel execution        | Router or SubAgents |
| Domains have conflicting instructions | SubAgents           |
| Need different models per domain      | SubAgents           |
| Sequential handoff workflow           | Handoffs            |

## Skills vs SubAgents

| Aspect       | Skills                  | SubAgents                   |
|--------------|-------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Architecture | Single agent            | Multiple agents             |
| Context      | Shared (weak isolation) | Separate (strong isolation) |

| Parallelism    | Not supported               | Supported                 |
|----------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------|
| Latency        | Lower (no routing)          | Higher (supervisor calls) |
| Tool Selection | Can degrade with many tools | Focused per subagent      |

## Part 5: The Router Pattern

## What Is the Router Pattern?

The Router pattern is where a classification step analyzes input, dispatches to specialized agents in parallel , and then synthesizes results into a unified response. It's optimized for queries that benefit from consulting multiple sources simultaneously.

## Real-World Analogy

## Library Research Desk:

1. You ask a complex question
2. Research coordinator analyzes your question
3. They dispatch researchers to different sections simultaneously
4. All researchers search in parallel
5. Coordinator synthesizes findings into one comprehensive answer

## Architecture Diagram

Architecture Diagram for Router Pattern

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## Key Characteristics

| Characteristic         | Description                                |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Classification First   | Router analyzes and decomposes the query   |
| Parallel Execution     | Multiple agents work simultaneously        |
| Targeted Sub-Questions | Each agent gets a domain-specific query    |
| Selective Routing      | Only relevant agents are invoked           |
| Result Synthesis       | All results combined into unified response |
| Typically Stateless    | Each request handled independently         |
| Context Isolation      | Each agent works in fresh context          |

Diagram comparing Sequential vs Parallel Latency

## Benefits

| Benefit            | Description                                   |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Parallel Execution | Significant latency reduction                 |
| Targeted Queries   | Each agent gets optimized sub-question        |
| Selective Routing  | Only relevant agents invoked                  |
| Clean Separation   | Classification, execution, synthesis distinct |
| Scalable           | Easy to add new agents                        |
| Predictable        | Explicit routing logic                        |

## Tradeoffs

| Tradeoff             | Impact                 |
|----------------------|------------------------|
| Stateless by Default | Each query independent |

| Classification Overhead   | Extra LLM call for routing       |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Rigid Flow                | Can't adjust mid-execution       |
| Synthesis Quality         | Depends on good synthesis prompt |
| No Agent Interaction      | Agents can't consult each other  |

## When to Use Router

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## ✅ Ideal Use Cases

| Use Case                    | Why Router Works                               |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Multi-source knowledge base | Parallel search across docs, code, discussions |
| Research queries            | Consult multiple databases simultaneously      |
| Comparison questions        | "Compare X across these sources"               |
| API aggregation             | Call multiple external APIs in parallel        |

## ❌ Not Suitable When

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

| Scenario                         | Better Pattern        |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------|
| Need multi-turn conversation     | Handoffs or SubAgents |
| Agents need to talk to user      | Handoffs              |
| Dynamic routing based on results | SubAgents             |
| Sequential workflow              | Handoffs              |

## Router vs SubAgents

| Aspect                      | Router                                          | SubAgents            |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| Classification (structured) | Supervisor reasoning (dynamic)                  | Routing Decision     |
| Once, upfront               | Continuously during                             | When Routing Happens |
| Native                      | Possible but                                    | Parallelism          |
| Typically stateless         | Naturally stateful                              | Multi-turn           |
| Best For                    | One-shot parallel queries Dynamic orchestration |                      |

## Selection Guide

## Choose SubAgents When:

- You need centralized orchestration with dynamic routing
- Specialists shouldn't talk to users directly
- You want context isolation between domains

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

- Conversation continuity is important
- You might need parallel execution

## Choose Handoffs When:

- Users should talk directly to specialists
- You have a sequential workflow to enforce
- State must persist across agent transitions
- Workflow feels like department transfers

## Choose Skills When:

- You want simplicity (single agent)
- Capabilities needed on-demand , not always
- Low latency is critical
- Domains don't have conflicting instructions

## Choose Router When:

- You need parallel queries to multiple sources
- Queries are mostly one-shot (not conversational)
- You want explicit classification logic
- Results need synthesis from multiple sources

## Summary

Multi-agent systems divide cognitive labor among specialized AI agents. The four main patterns each have distinct strengths:

| Pattern                                            | One-Line Summary   |
|----------------------------------------------------|--------------------|
| Supervisor coordinates specialists as tools        | SubAgents          |
| Handoffs Agents transfer control via state updates |                    |
| Skills Single agent loads capabilities on-demand   |                    |
| Router Classify →parallel dispatch →synthesize     |                    |

Start simple with a single agent, and evolve to multi-agent when you hit the triggers: tool overload, context limits, sequential constraints, parallelization needs, or organizational boundaries.

Choose your pattern based on:

- Who should talk to the user?
- Do you need parallel execution?
- Is it conversational or one-shot?
- How isolated should contexts be?

The right pattern depends on your specific requirements - there's no universal "best" choice.
